newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Two letter bombs found at United Nations.
newsitem.headline: Two letter bombs found at United Nations.

text.p: Two letter bombs were found at U.N. headquarters on Monday, addressed to the U.N. bureau of the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat. Both were rendered harmless, a U.N. spokesman said.
Earlier in the day, a letter bomb exploded at the same newspaper's London office, wounding two security guards. Four more suspect devices were subsequently found there, British police said.

After the first suspicious envelope was discovered in a messenger room at U.N. headquarters, parts of two floors of the 38-storey complex were closed off and the New York police bomb squad was called in.
U.N. security chief Michael McCann said the device was found to be a letter bomb. It arrived at U.N. headquarters on Friday or Saturday in a white greeting-card sized envelope addressed to Al-Hayat.
It was similar to several letter bombs mailed earlier this month to the same Saudi Arabian-owned newspaper's Washington bureau.
U.N. officials declined to give further details of the device because of an investigation. But other sources said that, like those received in Washington, it bore an Alexandria, Egypt, postmark.
"It was a live bomb and it was rendered safe in the (U.N. basement) garage," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said of the first device.

A few hours later he told reporters that "another letter bomb was found in the basement mail room" and that it was "very similar in format" to the first one and addressed to Al-Hayat also. The New York police bomb squad was again summoned.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan issued a statement after the discovery of the first bomb, saying it was "a reminder of the dangerous conditions under which many journalists must work."

"The secretary-general unreservedly condemns this cowardly act which is an assault on the United Nations itself and on the principle of free expression for which the United Nations stands," the statement added.

The first letter bomb, of a type which explodes when the envelope is opened, had not been detected in the basement area where mail is first sorted, but after it reached a messenger station on the second floor, Eckhard said.
It was addressed to Al-Hayat's bureau, not to any specific individual.
The evacuation of part of the press area resulted in a 90-minute delay in the U.N. spokesman's daily news conference.

A U.N. source said mail delivered to the United Nations was normally scanned as a security precaution. The precautions were stepped up after Al-Hayat's U.N. correspondent, Raghida Dergham, informed U.N. security of the London incident.
"We at Al-Hayat do not have any particular suspect," Dergham said. "We are going to go on with our very independent reporting," she added.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation launched an investigation earlier this month after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States.
Four arrived at Al-Hayat's Washington office and a fifth was found in the mail system. Three other devices turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas.
